Etched went from $10.3B to $21B in 26 days.

The obvious lesson is about AI infrastructure.

The more useful lesson is about sequencing.

Etched did not suddenly become valuable because it announced another funding round.

Before the latest repricing, several things had happened:

Its chip had been manufactured successfully.

The company said it had more than $1B in customer contracts.

It raised $300M at a $10.3B valuation in July.

Then Jane Street tested the hardware, became the first customer, and deployed a rack.

A few weeks later, investors priced the company at $21B.

The order matters.

A lot of founders try to raise conviction with bigger claims.

Take a crypto infrastructure company raising right now.

Good product. Real engineering. The kind of custody infrastructure that takes an hour to explain properly. The deck shows it. Forty-some slides, most of them architecture.

Partners keep passing after the second meeting. Nobody says why.

The founders assume the answer is more detail. More proof the tech is real. So the deck keeps getting longer.

What they're missing: the person in the room is rarely the person who says yes. The story has to survive being retold on Monday by someone who half remembers it. Complexity doesn't survive that trip. Clarity does.
